title: The Responsibility of Those Who Can See
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Schafer argues that clarity in leadership creates obligation: once a leader recognises what is really happening, silence becomes a form of participation in what no longer works. She distinguishes visibility, being seen commenting or reacting, from responsibility, which means staying engaged after attention fades. Anchoring the argument in the Los Angeles fires recovery, she says honest but uncomfortable truths, such as some areas not being safe to rebuild as before, go unspoken and so shift costs to the powerless. She asks leaders to speak gently, steadily and consistently and to help create conditions for solutions rather than simply pointing out problems. The piece closes with her organisation's role and reflection questions, so it is partly a statement of mission.
points: Awareness creates obligation, so seeing clearly and staying silent is a choice with consequences.
Visibility is about being seen, whereas responsibility is about staying accountable over the longer view.
Avoiding hard truths does not remove them but transfers the cost to those with least power.
Leaders should speak gently, steadily and consistently rather than loudly or dramatically.
The reflection questions turn the argument into a personal test of which truths you are avoiding.
quotes: Seeing clearly is not a neutral experience. Once we recognize what is actually happening, we are no longer simply observers. Awareness creates obligation. To see and remain silent is to participate, however unintentionally, in maintaining what no longer works.
Visibility is about being seen. Responsibility is about being accountable.

Responsibility, however, belongs to those willing to hold the longer view to remain engaged after attention fades, to speak again when silence would be easier, and to help create conditions for solutions rather than simply pointing out problems.
And yet, not saying them does not make the reality disappear; it simply transfers the cost to those with the least power to absorb it.

Those who can see patterns, root causes, long-term consequences, often wish they could look away. Not because they lack care, but because what they see is complex, disruptive, and rarely accompanied by an easy solution.

Our work is not to prescribe answers or rush outcomes, but to create the conditions where truth can be spoken, heard, and held long enough for real solutions to emerge. To convene people across sectors.
